governedRules.filing: File with the clerk of the convicting district court, docketed in the original criminal action, with the Criminal Cover Sheet and the required number of copies. Confirm the copy count with the clerk before filing.
governedRules.fees: Docket fee $176 under K.S.A. 21-6614(g)(2). The supreme court may additionally impose a charge not exceeding $19 per case to fund non-judicial personnel; 2026 Senate Bill 430 carries that authority from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2030. The docket fee is the only fee that may be collected for the case.
governedRules.feeWaiver: None in this lane. The only fee waiver in K.S.A. 21-6614 is the specialty court waiver at (a)(3). 2026 House Bill 2724, which would have authorised judges to waive the expungement docket fee on a poverty affidavit, died without enactment, so no general poverty-based statutory waiver exists. Some district courts nonetheless accept a poverty affidavit in practice.
governedRules.notice: The court sets the hearing date and causes notice to be given to the prosecutor and the arresting law enforcement agency, K.S.A. 21-6614(g)(1). No response or objection period is specified; the prosecutor appears at the hearing.
governedRules.service: The participant files the Notice of Hearing with the original plus two copies and the clerk sends them to the prosecutor and the arresting law enforcement agency. The participant does not serve and does not sign the certificate.
governedRules.participantSignature: The petitioner signs the petition, affirming under penalty of perjury that the statements are accurate to the best of their knowledge.

governedGenerationRequirements.question: What is your full legal name?
What was your full name at the time of the arrest, conviction or diversion, if different from your name now?
What sex, race and date of birth should the petition state?
In which Kansas county and which court was the case, and what is the case number?
Which law enforcement agency arrested you?
What offence were you convicted of, and under which Kansas statute?
On what date was the offence committed? This is not the same as the conviction date, and it decides which version of the law applies to you.
On what date were you convicted?
How was the offence classified — a traffic, cigarette or tobacco infraction, a misdemeanour, or a felony? If a felony, what class or grid severity level?
Was the conviction for driving under the influence under K.S.A. 8-1567, and if so was it a first violation or a second or subsequent violation?
On what date did you satisfy the sentence imposed?
On what date were you discharged from probation, a community correctional services programme, parole, postrelease supervision, conditional release or a suspended sentence?
Have you been convicted of a felony in the past two years, or is any felony proceeding pending or being instituted against you?
Are you currently required to register under the Kansas Offender Registration Act?
Having read the list of offences that cannot be expunged, do you assert that your conviction is not one of them and is not comparable to one of them under a pre-July-2011 offence definition?
In your own words: what has changed in your circumstances and behaviour since the case, and why does expungement matter to you now?
What documents do you have that show what you have been doing since the case — employment, education, treatment, service, letters of support?

selfHelpStopDisclosures.condition: The court sets a contested evidentiary hearing or a person appears to testify against the petition.
The offence classification or severity level is disputed.
The State v. Anderson time-of-offence analysis is in play beyond the DUI rows in the Judicial Council chart.
The participant may currently be required to register under the Kansas Offender Registration Act.
The record may be comparable to a K.S.A. 21-6614(e) offence under paragraph (19).
The participant needs to build a real showing on the (h)(2), (h)(3) or (h)(4) findings.
The petition seeks expungement of a felony conviction, because of the firearms-safety finding at (h)(4).
The participant is seeking firearms restoration as the primary goal, which is a federal and state law question beyond the order.
The arrest county and the convicting county differ.
